identification.summary: Lilac Typhoon is the Microsoft name for the threat actor it earlier tracked as DEV-0234, with China as its listed origin [S4]. In June 2022 Microsoft named DEV-0234 and DEV-0401 among the 'multiple adversaries and nation-state actors' exploiting the Atlassian Confluence remote code execution flaw CVE-2022-26134 [S1][S2][S3]. Public reporting on the actor beyond this one Microsoft mention is very limited.
identification.firstObserved: Earliest public reference found: Microsoft Threat Intelligence post of 2022-06-11 naming DEV-0234 as exploiting CVE-2022-26134 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft maps Lilac Typhoon to DEV-0234 only; it lists no other vendor names [S4]. Third-party profiles (Malpedia, Strobes) repeat the DEV-0234 alias and the China attribution and cite the June 2022 Microsoft post [S6]. In the same June 2022 statement Microsoft named DEV-0401, which SecurityWeek describes as a separate China-based ransomware operator (LockFile, AtomSilo, Rook) [S3]. Keep DEV-0401 activity separate from Lilac Typhoon. The payload list commonly attached to this actor (Cobalt Strike, web shells, botnets, coin miners, ransomware including Cerber2021) describes everything Microsoft saw across all CVE-2022-26134 exploitation. It is not attributed to DEV-0234 specifically [S2][S3].

attribution.sponsor: China (Microsoft 'Origin/Threat' designation) [S4]. No public source found names a specific PRC organization (MSS, PLA, MPS) or contractor.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft lists the origin as China [S4] and grouped DEV-0234 with the 'nation-state actors' exploiting CVE-2022-26134 [S1]. Microsoft did not publish a confidence level in the sources found. No government attribution of DEV-0234 or Lilac Typhoon was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry, reported in a 2022-06-11 social media post [S1] and covered by trade press [S2][S3], plus Microsoft's naming mapping [S4]. No technical report on this actor was found.

sectors: Organizations running internet-facing Atlassian Confluence Server or Data Center (cross-sector) [S1][S5]
targeting.notes: The only documented targeting is opportunistic exploitation of vulnerable Confluence Server/Data Center instances in June 2022 [S1][S2]. Confluence Cloud was not affected [S7]. No victims, sectors or regions attributable to DEV-0234 specifically were found in public sources.

capabilities.summary: Microsoft reported that DEV-0234 exploited CVE-2022-26134 [S1][S2][S3]. That flaw is an unauthenticated OGNL-injection remote code execution vulnerability in Confluence Server and Data Center, patched by Atlassian on 2022-06-03 [S5][S7]. Microsoft said exploitation of the flaw across all actors delivered Cobalt Strike, web shells, botnets (Mirai, Kinsing), coin miners and ransomware (Cerber2021) [S2][S3]. Microsoft did not state which of these payloads DEV-0234 used. The actor quickly weaponized an n-day edge/collaboration-server vulnerability within about a week of disclosure [S1][S7]. That is the only capability the sources support.

campaigns.name: Exploitation of Atlassian Confluence CVE-2022-26134
campaigns.summary: Microsoft named DEV-0234 (now Lilac Typhoon) and DEV-0401 among the adversaries and nation-state actors exploiting the Confluence OGNL-injection RCE flaw shortly after Atlassian's 2022-06-03 patch. Across all actors, observed payloads included Cobalt Strike, web shells, botnets, coin miners and Cerber2021 ransomware.

diamond.adversary: China-origin actor tracked by Microsoft as Lilac Typhoon (formerly DEV-0234) [S4]; no named individuals or units in public sources.
diamond.capability: Exploitation of Confluence CVE-2022-26134 (unauthenticated OGNL-injection RCE) [S1][S5]; specific post-exploitation tooling not attributed [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Internet-exposed Confluence Server/Data Center instances (opportunistic) [S1][S5]; no named victims.
diamond.technology: On-premises Atlassian Confluence Server and Data Center versions before the June 2022 fixes [S5][S7].

gaps: No Microsoft blog post or technical report specific to DEV-0234/Lilac Typhoon was found. Its public record rests on a single 2022-06-11 Microsoft post and press coverage of it [S1][S2][S3].

Microsoft did not say which CVE-2022-26134 payloads (Cobalt Strike, web shells, coin miners, botnets, Cerber2021) DEV-0234 used. The imported summary's statement that this actor deployed all of them is not supported at actor level.
Whether DEV-0234 is espionage-motivated, financially motivated or both is unknown. Microsoft's 'nation-state actors' phrasing covers the group of actors named, not DEV-0234 specifically.

The imported reference (Security Boulevard coverage of CISA/NSA/FBI advisory AA22-279A, Oct 2022) could not be opened. Whether that advisory lists CVE-2022-26134 among CVEs exploited by PRC state-sponsored actors was not verified, and the advisory does not name Lilac Typhoon or DEV-0234 in any source seen.
The imported Risky Business newsletter reference could not be opened; its relevance is unverified.

Volexity first detected in-the-wild CVE-2022-26134 exploitation, which involved BEHINDER and China Chopper web shells [S7]. Nothing in the sources links that intrusion to DEV-0234, so it is not merged here.
No overlaps with other vendors' clusters are published (no MITRE ATT&CK group ID). Third-party profiles (Malpedia) appear to restate the Microsoft post [S6].
Activity after 2022 under the Lilac Typhoon name was not found in public reporting.
Primary pages from therecord.media, securityweek.com and malpedia could not be fetched (network blocked); their content was taken from search-result excerpts.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): internet-facing on-premises Confluence and similar collaboration servers on DoD, DIB and mission-partner networks are relevant key terrain, because they store planning and engineering documentation [S1][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): an unauthenticated RCE gives the actor immediate server-level access, and mass exploitation started within days of disclosure, so the defender has very little time to patch [S1][S7]. STEP 3 (threat model): the evidenced template is opportunistic exploitation of a public n-day in a collaboration server [S1][S2]. Follow-on tooling for this actor is undocumented; across actors it included web shells, Cobalt Strike, coin miners and ransomware [S2][S3]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is opportunistic exploitation of newly disclosed edge or collaboration-server RCEs to gain footholds. MDCOA is persistent access to unpatched collaboration servers holding operational planning data, used for collection or handed off to other PRC actors. Candidate indicators: OGNL-injection patterns in Confluence request URIs, new JSP/web-shell files in Confluence directories, Confluence service processes spawning shells or downloaders, and unexpected outbound connections from Confluence hosts [S5][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track the exposure and patch state of collaboration servers (Confluence and similar) in JCC2 views. Treat CISA KEV additions such as CVE-2022-26134 as triggers for an immediate exposure check [S7]. (2) Authorities: Microsoft's DEV-0234 attribution is a vendor assessment without government corroboration, so response actions should rest on observed exploitation, not on the actor name [S1][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: account for internal wikis and knowledge bases that hold mission data when assessing compromise impact. (4) Coordination: many criminal and state actors exploited the same flaw [S2][S3]. Deconflict attribution with DC3/DIB CS partners and CISA, and prioritize containment over actor naming.
